# ALife

Spatial artificial life: grid cellular automata (life-like, cyclic and Wolfram's elementary rules), continuous systems (reaction-diffusion, Turing patterns, Lenia), agent populations (boids, Physarum, diffusion-limited aggregation) and structural growth (L-systems, space colonization), plus the measurement layer every one of them makes its claims through.

9 source file(s), 420 public symbol(s), 229 of them carrying KDoc. Everything below is the documentation that lives beside the code — the same text the [completion documentation panel](../completion_doc_browser.md) shows in the editor. A blank summary means the declaration has no KDoc yet, not that this page dropped it.

## alife.kt { #alife-kt }

Spatial artificial life for the Field stdlib — the *continuous / grid / agent* half of ALife, the
counterpart to the graph-rewriting half already here (`growing.kt`, `dynamic_graph_systems.kt`,
`interactionnets.kt`, `booleannetworks.kt`) and to the constraint-based generator in `wfc.kt`.

Six files:

- **`alife.kt`** (this one) — the substrate: [`IntGrid`](alife.md#alife-kt-intgrid), the grid↔[`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) bridges, and the
  **measurement** layer. Everything else in the family makes its claims through the functions at
  the bottom of this file.
- **`alife_ca.kt`** — discrete cellular automata: [`LifeRule`](alife.md#alife-ca-kt-liferule) parsed from `B3/S23`, outer-totalistic
  and cyclic multi-state CA, Wolfram's elementary 1-D rules rendered as a space-time [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img), and a
  3-D life-like CA that marches out to a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh).
- **`alife_continuous.kt`** — Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion, Turing patterns, and Lenia
  (continuous CA: ring-kernel convolution plus a growth mapping).
- **`alife_field.kt`** — the inline `ToHTML` views for [`IntGrid`](alife.md#alife-kt-intgrid), `GrayScottState` and `LeniaRun`,
  kept separate so the five system files name nothing from Field's visualizer.
- **`alife_agents.kt`** — boids flocking, a Physarum/slime-mould deposit–sense–move population over
  a trail [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img), and diffusion-limited aggregation.
- **`alife_lsystem.kt`** — a bracketed/parametric L-system with a turtle that emits
  `afield.graphics.FLine`s, and space-colonization branching.

Design choices, all deliberate:

- **Built on [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img), not on a private raster.** Every continuous system is an `Img -> Img` step, so a
  reaction–diffusion field pipelines straight into `gaussianBlur`, `colormap`, `connectedComponents`,
  `isoContourFLines` and `asHeightSdf` with no glue. Nothing here reimplements convolution.
- **A step is a value, not a side effect.** `step()` returns the next state; you keep the frames you
  want. The one exception is the mutable agent populations, where copying 50 000
  agents per frame would be the whole cost.
- **Deterministic from a seed.** Every stochastic system takes a `seed: Long` and uses its own
  `kotlin.random.Random`, so a figure in the docs is reproducible and a regression is a diff.
- **No external dependency.** Pure Kotlin over `FloatArray`/`IntArray`.
- **Measured, not asserted.** The functions under "Measurement" exist because "it produced pixels"
  is not evidence. A flock is a population whose `polarization` is high *and* whose
  `nearestNeighborDistances` have a floor; a DLA cluster is one whose `massRadiusDimension` is
  ~1.7; a Gray–Scott spot regime is one whose `blobShapes` are round. Each of those is a number a
  control arm gets wrong.

Out of scope: GPU implementations (that is `afield.four` / StackSL / RectSL — these are
CPU reference implementations you can read), and any system needing a trained model.

## alife_agents.kt { #alife-agents-kt }

Agent-based spatial ALife: boids flocking, a Physarum (slime-mould) deposit–sense–move population
over a trail [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img), and diffusion-limited aggregation.

See `alife.kt` for the family overview.

These are the three canonical demonstrations that **global order can have no global rule**: a flock's
alignment, a slime mould's transport network and a dendrite's fractal dimension are all properties
nothing in the code mentions. Which is exactly why each one here ships with a control arm — a run of
the same code with one interaction switched off — because "emergence" is otherwise the easiest thing
in computing to claim and the hardest to check. See `polarization`, `Img.topShare` and
`massRadiusDimension` for the three numbers those controls fail.

Unlike the rest of the family these types are **mutable**: `step()` advances the population in place.
Copying 50 000 agents per frame would be the entire cost of a Physarum run, and the systems are
simulations rather than values.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/alife_agents.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/alife_agents/)

**Used in:** [Spatial artificial life](../alife_examples.md)

## alife_animate.kt { #alife-animate-kt }

One shared way to *animate* the `alife*.kt` family — because every system in it is a time
evolution, and a montage of frozen generations is the one view that hides the thing they are about.

The whole file is `Box.animateEvolution` plus four small "show a prefix of something" helpers. It sits
apart from the five simulation files for the same reason `alife_field.kt` does: those files name nothing
from Field's box runtime, and this one is entirely about it (`Box`, `Frames`, `display`).

**Pacing is the craft, and it is the reason this is a shared helper rather than a copied loop.** The
naive animation — one simulation step per displayed frame — is wrong for almost every system here, and
wrong in two opposite directions:

 - Gray–Scott needs about **6000** explicit-Euler steps to reach its named regime. One step per frame at
   20 fps is five minutes of a clip in which nothing happens.
 - Conway's glider moves one cell per **four** generations. Forty steps per frame is a strobe.

So `Box.animateEvolution` takes the *whole* evolution — `totalSteps` — and the `seconds` it should occupy,
and derives the steps per displayed frame. Live playback uses monotonic time. Frame-synchronous recording
installs an `AnimationClock` whose time is exactly `frameIndex / fps`, so the same seed produces the same
ordered simulation states even when browser painting or encoding is slow. Capture performance changes how
long the build takes, never which states enter the movie.

**A linear step schedule is not a neutral choice, and for some of these systems it is the wrong one.**
Reaction–diffusion and Lenia are *log-time* processes: the visible change from step 60 to step 600 is
about the same as from step 600 to step 6000. Spend equal steps on equal wall-clock and the clip
front-loads — measured as the mean absolute luma difference between the extracted frames of the
Gray–Scott clip on `alife_examples.md`, a linear schedule gave **42.09** from the first frame to the
middle and **3.98** from the middle to the last: the reader watches it finish and then waits. So
`Box.animateEvolution` takes a `ramp`, and the schedule it drives is geometric rather than linear. See
that parameter for the arithmetic.

**The step counter belongs in the frame.** Every call site here labels its panels with the step number,
which is not decoration: it is how "did this clip actually reach the regime?" is answered by *looking* at
the last frame of the recorded mp4 rather than by trusting the schedule. A clip whose final label reads
`step 2100 / 6000` is a failed clip, and it says so on its face.

**The range policy from `alife_field.kt` applies with more force here, not less.** A colour map whose
range is taken from the frame makes an animation of a growing structure appear to stand still, and makes
a saturating field indistinguishable from a dying one. So every call site passes explicit `lo`/`hi` to
`Img.colormap`. Auto-ranging is a per-figure mistake and a per-*frame* lie.

## alife_ca.kt { #alife-ca-kt }

Discrete cellular automata: life-like and outer-totalistic rules on a 2-D lattice, cyclic
multi-state CA, Wolfram's elementary 1-D rules as a space-time raster, and a 3-D life-like CA that
marches out to a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh).

See `alife.kt` for the family overview and for [`IntGrid`](alife.md#alife-kt-intgrid), the lattice everything here steps.

The design commitment worth stating: a *rule* is a value ([`LifeRule`](alife.md#alife-ca-kt-liferule)), separate from the grid it is
applied to. That is what lets the gallery run the same glider under `B3/S23` and under a
deliberately-wrong neighbour rule and show that only one of them translates — and what lets
`alife_continuous.kt`'s Lenia stepper be checked against this file's discrete stepper in the limit
where the two must agree.

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">LifeRule</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">birth</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Set</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">survive</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Set</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">vonNeumann</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">notation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">&quot;B${birth.sorted().joinToString(&quot;</span><span class="s">&quot;)}/S${survive.sorted().joinToString(&quot;</span><span class="s">&quot;)}&quot;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/alife_ca/#L39)

## alife_continuous.kt { #alife-continuous-kt }

Continuous spatial ALife: reaction–diffusion (Gray–Scott / Turing) and Lenia, all shaped as
`Img -> Img` steps so they compose with the imaging family.

See `alife.kt` for the family overview.

Every system here is a **field**, not a lattice of labels, so the measurements that matter are
different from the discrete half: not "is this pattern periodic" but "what shape are its features"
(`Img.blobShapes`) and "what length scale did it choose" (`Img.correlationLength`). The one exception,
and the reason the two halves live in the same family, is `leniaFromLifeRule`: Lenia in its discrete
limit *is* a life-like CA, and that gives this file's float convolution and `alife_ca.kt`'s integer
neighbour counting a claim they must agree on exactly.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/alife_continuous.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/alife_continuous/)

**Used in:** [Spatial artificial life](../alife_examples.md)

## alife_evolve.kt { #alife-evolve-kt }

The search half of this family: rule sets as **genomes**, the measurements in `alife.kt` as
**fitness**, and `PopulationSearch` as the engine that connects them.

Until this file existed every figure on the ALife page was "run a fixed rule and measure it". The
measuring vocabulary was already here and was already good — `stateEntropyBits`,
`massRadiusDimension`, `blobShapes`, `translationBetween`, `LeniaRun.centroidDrift` — and each of
those is a fitness function with nobody calling it. This file supplies the missing halves: a
[`GenomeOps`](search.md#populationsearch-kt-genomeops) for three families ([`LifeRuleGenome`](alife.md#alife-evolve-kt-liferulegenome), [`LeniaGenome`](alife.md#alife-evolve-kt-leniagenome), [`LSystemGenome`](alife.md#alife-evolve-kt-lsystemgenome)) and an
[`Objective`](search.md#populationsearch-kt-objective) for each, assembled out of statistics that were already in the file next door.

There is **no search code here**. Every driver comes from [`PopulationSearch`](search.md#populationsearch-kt-populationsearch), which is also what
`FunctionEvolve.evolve` runs on. That is the point: one engine, several genomes, rather than a
third private optimizer.

**Every objective in this file evaluates every candidate from the same fixed initial condition.**
A Lenia rule is seeded from `leniaSeed(..., seed = initialSeed)`, a CA rule from the same
`randomSoup`, an L-system from the same axiom. A search that re-randomised the initial condition
per candidate would be selecting on the luck of the draw, and the resulting "improvement" would be
mostly the search rediscovering that some soups are easier than others. Where robustness across
initial conditions *is* the question, `caEdgeOfChaosObjective` takes several soups and reports one
`Evaluation.cases` entry each, which is what makes `Selection.LEXICASE` meaningful here.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/alife_evolve.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/alife_evolve/)

**Used in:** [Spatial artificial life](../alife_examples.md)

## alife_field.kt { #alife-field-kt }

Inline `ToHTML` views for the `alife*.kt` family — what a box draws when you *evaluate* an [`IntGrid`](alife.md#alife-kt-intgrid)
or a [`GrayScottState`](alife.md#alife-continuous-kt-grayscottstate), with nothing to set up.

`alife.kt` and `alife_continuous.kt` name only the three entry points here (`alifeGridHtml`,
`alifeGrayScottHtml`, `alifeLeniaRunHtml`), each from a one-line `toHTML` override, and inherit
every pixel of their view from them.

**The range policy:**

 - **Every scale is named in the caption**, with both endpoints spelled out in the units of the
   thing being shown.
 - **Domains are fixed by meaning, not by the frame.** An [`IntGrid`](alife.md#alife-kt-intgrid)'s states run `0 .. maxState`; a
   Gray–Scott `v` runs `0 .. 1`, the range the reaction is defined on, *not* `min .. max` of this
   particular field. Auto-range a saturated Lenia field — constant at 1 — and it maps to the bottom
   of the ramp: solid black, identical to a field that has died.
 - **One pixel per cell, never resampled.** The `<img>` is scaled by an integer factor with
   `image-rendering:pixelated`, so cell coordinates and pixel coordinates stay the same thing and a
   reader can count. A filtered upscale destroys exactly the local structure a CA is about.
 - **A flat field says so.** If every cell holds the same value the caption reports it, because a
   uniform panel is otherwise indistinguishable from a broken one.

`AlifeGallery`'s `inline-view` figure decodes the base64 PNG back out of the emitted HTML and
asserts the colour of individual pixels against the value the caption claims for them.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/alife_field.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/alife_field/)

## alife_lsystem.kt { #alife-lsystem-kt }

Structural spatial ALife: a bracketed, parametric, optionally stochastic L-system with a turtle that
emits `FLine`s, plus space-colonization branching.

See `alife.kt` for the family overview.

L-systems are the odd one out in this family and belong in it for a precise reason: they are the one
generative system here whose output can be checked **exactly and combinatorially** rather than
statistically. Lindenmayer's original algae system has Fibonacci-length derivations; the Koch
*snowflake* has exactly `3 * 4^n` forward symbols after `n` rewrites (the quadratic Koch island this
file also ships, `LSYSTEM_KOCH_QUADRATIC`, has `5^n` — check which one you are asserting about); the
Koch snowflake's turtle path closes to a
measurable area. Those are equalities, not distributions, so they are the sharpest evidence in the
whole family — and they exercise the same turtle that draws the pretty trees.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/alife_lsystem.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/stdlib/alife_lsystem/)

**Used in:** [Spatial artificial life](../alife_examples.md)
